source: Source: Robert Shiller (Yale) US stock data; FRED. Real total returns, 1871–2026

slides.h1: Does “Sell in May and go away” actually work?
slides.p: 155 years of US stock market data, month by month.
Average return after inflation, May–Oct vs Nov–Apr. But the gap’s 95% confidence interval runs from −0.3 to +4.5 points.
slides.small: Winter beat the summer before it in only 52% of years

slides.h2: But a weak summer still usually beats cash
slides.p: of summers, stocks beat Treasury bills. Staying invested earned 2.4% more than cash on average.
slides.small: Selling in May swaps summer stocks for summer cash, not for winter

slides.p: Buy and hold. Switching to cash every May and back in November: $3,555, before costs and tax.

slides.h2: Winter minus summer, by era (percentage points)
slides.p: Since 2002 switching trailed holding by 2.7 points a year.

slides.h2: To be fair to the idea
items: Smaller crashes: worst real fall 57%, vs 77% for holding
It beat a constant half stocks, half cash mix: 5.4% vs 4.75% a year
But a cost of about 0.31% per switch wipes that edge out
Tax makes it far worse outside an ISA or pension

slides.p: Pick the months, the period and the trading costs, and compare switching with holding.
slides.small: Not financial advice. Past returns don’t guarantee future ones.
